Where it began

Kirti Azad was born in Purnia, in Bihar, on 2 January 1959. He went to Modern School in Delhi, where he played in the school team, and then to the University of Delhi.

He batted right-handed and bowled off-spin, and for many seasons he was one of the men Delhi relied on with both. In 95 Ranji Trophy matches he made 4,867 runs at 47.72 and took 162 wickets at 28.91. The highest of his scores was 215, made against Himachal Pradesh in the 1985-86 season.

The player

India surprised plenty of people by taking him on their 1980-81 trip to Australia and New Zealand, and he made his Test debut at Wellington. He played three more Tests against England in 1981-82, and seven in all between 1981 and 1983, making 135 runs with a best of 24 and taking three wickets.

The great day came in the one-day game. He was a member of the India squad that won the 1983 World Cup. His one-day international career ran through most of the 1980s, with 25 matches in all.

What made him special

At domestic level he gave Delhi two cricketers for the price of one: a batter who could go on to a double hundred and an off-spinner who could take wickets by the dozen. An average of 47.72 over 95 Ranji matches is a record most batters would be proud of.

Test cricket never quite saw that player. The runs and wickets that came so easily for Delhi were harder to find at the highest level, and his three Test wickets cost 124.33 each. Seven caps and a World Cup winner's medal, though, are more than most domestic heroes ever get.

Away from the middle

Years after he stopped playing, he turned up on the big screen. In 2019 he played the lead role, as himself, in the film Kirket, and in 83, the 2021 film about the World Cup win, the actor Dinker Sharma played him.

And finally

There cannot be many cricketers who have both played themselves in one film and been played by somebody else in another. He had the advantage, at least, of knowing exactly how the part should go.
